answers.label: B
answers.working:
Hot concentrated sulphuric acid oxidises carbon to carbon dioxide and is itself reduced to sulphur dioxide:

\(\mathrm{C + 2H_2SO_4 \longrightarrow CO_2 + 2SO_2 + 2H_2O}\)

Both \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) turn lime water milky, so two such gases are formed. Sulphur gives only one gas (\(\mathrm{SO_2}\)), and oxygen and nitrogen do not react in this way.

So the answer is option (B), carbon.

An ionic bond forms between a metal that loses electrons easily and a non-metal that gains electrons easily. Group 2 elements (such as magnesium) lose two electrons and Group 17 elements (halogens such as chlorine) gain one electron each, giving an ionic compound like \(\mathrm{MgCl_2}\).

Pair P is two groups of metals, pair Q (for example carbon and oxygen) forms covalent bonds, and Group 18 noble gases in pair S do not form bonds at all.

So the answer is option (C), R.

answers.value: Copper metal is deposited at the negative electrode.
answers.working:
With copper electrodes the anode is an active electrode. At the cathode (negative electrode) copper ions gain electrons and copper is deposited, so the cathode gains mass: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \longrightarrow Cu}\).

At the anode (positive electrode) copper atoms lose electrons and go into solution, so the anode loses mass and no oxygen is given off: \(\mathrm{Cu - 2e^- \longrightarrow Cu^{2+}}\).

This makes options (B), (C) and (D) wrong. So the answer is option (A), copper metal is deposited at the negative electrode.

In diffused sunlight or ultraviolet light, chlorine replaces one hydrogen atom of ethane (a substitution reaction). The hydrogen atom that is removed combines with the other chlorine atom to form hydrogen chloride:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_6 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{UV\ light} C_2H_5Cl + HCl}\)

The product is chloroethane. A saturated compound like ethane cannot simply add chlorine as in option (A).

So the answer is option (C). Note: the option is printed as \(\mathrm{C_2H_5CI}\) (capital I); it means \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\), chloroethane.

answers.label: D
answers.working:
Metals above hydrogen in the activity series displace hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid; metals below hydrogen do not.

- Copper is below hydrogen, so no gas is given off. Observation 1 is wrong.
- Iron reacts: \(\mathrm{Fe + 2HCl \longrightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2}\). Observation 2 is correct.
- Magnesium reacts vigorously and gives hydrogen. Observation 3 is wrong.
- Zinc reacts: \(\mathrm{Zn + 2HCl \longrightarrow ZnCl_2 + H_2}\). Observation 4 is correct.

So the answer is option (D), both 2 and 4.

Atomic number 16 (2,8,6) gains electrons to form a negative ion, 10 is the noble gas neon, and 14 (2,8,4) shares electrons instead of forming ions.

Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from a dilute acid. A copper salt therefore cannot be made by the action of a dilute acid on copper metal.

Copper salts can be made from copper(II) oxide or hydroxide (bases) and from copper carbonate, for example \(\mathrm{CuO + 2HCl \longrightarrow CuCl_2 + H_2O}\).

So the answer is option (C), 3 (action of dilute acid on metals).

answers.working:
Sodium chloride is an ionic (electrovalent) compound. Its ions are held in a crystal lattice by strong electrostatic forces, so a lot of energy is needed to melt it (about \(801^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)).

Methane, ammonia and ethanol are covalent compounds with weak forces between their molecules, so they have low melting points.

So the answer is option (B), sodium chloride.

Concentrated sulphuric acid contains very little water, so it is mostly present as un-ionised molecules and is a poor conductor. When it is diluted, water makes it ionise: \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4 \longrightarrow 2H^+ + SO_4^{2-}}\).

Dilute sulphuric acid therefore has many more free (mobile) ions, and it is these ions that carry the current. So the assertion is true, the reason is true, and the reason explains the assertion.

So the answer is option (C).

By Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes, gases react and form in simple whole-number ratios of volume, given by the coefficients of the balanced equation.

1 volume of \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\) gives 3 volumes of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\). So 5 litres of propane gives \(5 \times 3 = 15\) litres of carbon dioxide.

So the answer is option (B), 15 litres.

A hydrocarbon with 3 carbon atoms and 6 hydrogen atoms is \(\mathrm{C_3H_6}\). This fits the alkene formula \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}\), so it has one C=C double bond and is unsaturated: propene, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH_3}\).

Propyne is \(\mathrm{C_3H_4}\), propane is \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\) (saturated) and propanol contains oxygen.

So the answer is option (C), propene.

\(\mathrm{2H_2O \longrightarrow 2H_2 + O_2}\)

The reason states the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in water as 1 : 2 by volume. That is the wrong way round: water contains hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1 by volume. So the reason is false.

P loses one electron easily, so it is a Group 1 metal at the left of the period. Q forms covalent bonds by sharing, so it lies in the middle of the period (like carbon or silicon). R has high electronegativity, so it is a non-metal at the right of the period (a halogen).

**(a)** Reduction is the gain of electrons. **P** is a metal that has a strong tendency to lose electrons and almost no tendency to gain them, so P is the most difficult to reduce. (R gains electrons most easily.)

**(b)** Across a period the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so the atoms get smaller. **R**, being furthest to the right, has the smallest atomic radius.

**(c)** Ionization potential increases across a period, so in decreasing order: **R > Q > P**.

answers.value: (a) Ag+ + e- -> Ag (b) deposition would be too fast, giving an uneven, non-durable coat (c) AC reverses the electrodes, so the deposit would dissolve again (d) the silver anode gradually wears away (thins)
answers.working:
**(a)** At the cathode (the spoon), silver ions gain electrons and silver is deposited:

\(\mathrm{Ag^+ + e^- \longrightarrow Ag}\)

**(b)** Silver nitrate solution gives a high concentration of \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) ions, so silver would be deposited too quickly and the coating would be rough, uneven and would not stick well. Sodium argentocyanide, \(\mathrm{Na[Ag(CN)_2]}\), releases \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) ions slowly and steadily, which gives a smooth, even and long-lasting coat.

**(c)** Alternating current keeps reversing its direction, so each electrode would keep changing from cathode to anode. Silver deposited on the spoon in one half-cycle would dissolve back in the next, and no lasting coat would form. Direct current is needed so that the spoon always stays the cathode.

**(d)** At the anode, silver atoms lose electrons and go into the solution, \(\mathrm{Ag - e^- \longrightarrow Ag^+}\). So the **silver anode gradually becomes thinner (decreases in size and mass)**.

**(b)** Across a period the **nuclear charge increases** while the new electrons enter the **same shell**. So the atomic size **decreases**, and the nucleus attracts the shared pair of electrons in a bond more strongly. Hence electronegativity increases across a period.

**(a)** Electronegativity increases across a period, so the most electronegative element of Period 2 is **fluorine (F)**.

**(b)** Atomic size decreases across a period, so the largest atom of Period 3 is the first one, **sodium (Na)**. (The noble gas argon is not compared, as its size is measured differently.)

**(a)** **F** (fluorine). It has only two shells and the highest nuclear charge among the Period 2 elements given, so its atom is the smallest. (K and Ca have four shells; Li has two shells but a smaller nuclear charge than F.)

**(b)** **Ca** (calcium), configuration 2,8,8,2, has two valence electrons.

**(c)** **K** (potassium). Electropositive character increases down a group and decreases across a period, so potassium (Group 1, Period 4) loses its electron most easily. It is more electropositive than Li (higher in the group) and Ca (to its right).

**(a)** **L** (sodium chloride solution). Sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte and is completely dissociated into \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions, so the solute is present only as ions.

**(b)** **M** (distilled water). Pure water is practically un-ionised, so it contains only molecules.

**(c)** **K** (aqueous acetic acid). Acetic acid is a weak acid; it ionises partly and gives \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions, so its pH is less than 7. (It contains both ions and molecules.)
